rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This section expands the Moses and Pharaoh account from the command to confront Pharaoh through the drowning of Pharaoh and his army.
rows.anchor: This anecdote begins at the instant when Moses (sws) and Aaron (sws) were asked to go to the Pharaoh and ends on the destruction through drowning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account's episodes reassure the Prophet and his companions and instruct his opponents.
rows.anchor: Each and every part of this anecdote is a source of assurance to the Prophet (sws) and his companions and teaches a lesson to his rivals.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People enslaved by desire remain unmoved even by great miracles and awaken only when they see their fate.
rows.anchor: those who lose their ability to understand by becoming slaves to their desires are not influenced by the greatest of miracles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage recalls God's call to Moses on his return from Midian in the sacred valley of Tuwa, where he was appointed and sent to Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: while he was returning from Madyan, God spoke to him in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā. He was assigned messengerhood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about fearing God portrays Pharaoh and his people as extremely rebellious; the author paraphrases it as an uncontrolled rise in injustice without fear of God's wrath.
rows.anchor: Will these unjust people continue to increase in their rebelliousness in an uncontrolled manner and not fear God’s wrath?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This warning style conveys anger, yearning, rebuke, and the nearness of God's punishment.
rows.anchor: Anger, yearning, rebuke and the proximity of God’s scourge found in this style does not need any elaboration.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says other prophets warn their peoples in the same way later in this sūra.
rows.anchor: It will become evident from verses 125, 143, 162 and 178 ahead that other prophets too warned their nations in this way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' fear reflects sensitivity to the grave responsibility, and he had already understood how difficult it would be to speak truth before Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: this fear is an essential consequence of sensitivity towards this responsibility. Before departing for Madyan, he fully realized the extent of difficulty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the reassurance, both messengers are to proceed fearlessly with their duty.
rows.anchor: Both should fearlessly proceed to their duty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted Moses' request to include Aaron, as indicated here and stated explicitly elsewhere.
rows.anchor: but accepted his request regarding Aaron (sws) as is indicated here and explicitly mentioned at other instances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God decisively reassured Moses that the Copts would not kill him.
rows.anchor: God emphatically put to rest Moses’ fear that the Copts would kill him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's assurance of being with the two messengers is especially eloquent; the author compares it with the assurance of hearing and seeing in 20:46.
rows.anchor: sound assurance in a very eloquent manner. In verse 46 of S ūrah Ṭāhā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording that they are messengers of the Lord of the worlds identifies Aaron as Moses' assisting messenger.
rows.anchor: Aaron (sws) was a helper messenger to Moses (sws). Thus in verse 47 of S ūrah Ṭāhā it is stated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Presenting two messengers to Pharaoh conclusively communicates the truth; rejection after this is Pharaoh's own misfortune.
rows.anchor: not one, but two messengers have been sent to him by the Almighty. If even after this, he does not adopt the right attitude, it is his own misfortune.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah indicates Moses sought to take the Israelites to a desert animal-sacrifice festival three days away, though it does not identify the precise place.
rows.anchor: to celebrate the ‘īd festival of animal sacrifice to a place in the desert at a distance of three days. However, the exact place

rows.speaker: Imām Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī thinks Moses intended to take the Israelites to Makkah for pilgrimage and sacrifice; Islahi says he lacks Farāhī's arguments and is not fully convinced.
rows.anchor: My mentor, Imām Farāhī, thinks that Moses (sws) wanted to take them to Makkah for ḥajj and animal sacrifice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Along with warning Pharaoh, Moses' first directive was to organize the Israelites and revive their religion.
rows.anchor: Together with warning the Pharaoh, this is the first directive given to Moses (sws) for organizing the Israelites and for their religious revival.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah's lack of detail may mean Moses withheld the destination from Pharaoh or the Jews concealed it as self-interest, as they concealed Ishmael's and the Kaaba's histories.
rows.anchor: There can be two reasons for this lack of clarity in this specific matter in the Torah. Either Moses (sws) did not want to make this evident to the Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the expression meaning ‘send us out,’ the preposition bāʾ is omitted under a common linguistic rule.
rows.anchor: has been suppressed in accordance with a common linguistic principle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits that Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and his courtiers, warned them, and demanded that the Israelites be released with them.
rows.anchor: A part of the anecdote is suppressed before these verses: At God’s behest, Moses (sws) took his brother Aaron (sws) along with him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's arrogant reply follows from his inability to tolerate an Israelite making such an important demand of him.
rows.anchor: important demand from him. So with great arrogance he uttered the words referred to in the verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word translated ‘ungrateful’ means that; Pharaoh's vague ‘then did what you did’ refers to Moses killing the Copt, with deliberate ambiguity reflecting the gravity of the act.
rows.anchor: here means “ungrateful.” The words “then did what you did” refers to Moses’ slaying of the Copt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's implication is that Moses was raised by him, committed a crime against Pharaoh's people, yet now claims prophethood and demands the Israelites.
rows.anchor: in spite of being raised by him and in spite of committing a crime against his nation, he is claiming to be a Prophet and demanding the Israelites go with him!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ḍāll here means ‘searching for the truth,’ as it does in 93:7.
rows.anchor: here means “in search of the truth,” the way it is used in verse 7 of Sūrah Ḍuhā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses openly acknowledges killing the Copt; after God's guidance and appointment as messenger, his present status differs entirely from his past, so Pharaoh must hear him without dwelling on the past.
rows.anchor: It is evident from this verse that Moses (sws) openly confessed to the killing of the Copt in the words it mentions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The killing was involuntary and arose from noble sympathy with an oppressed person; Moses was deeply grieved, repented, and was forgiven by God.
rows.anchor: This happened absolutely involuntarily merely with the noble emotions of helping an oppressed person. Moses (sws) was stricken with extreme grief after it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets are upright before being chosen, but uprightness and intellect cannot by themselves guide a person through life's uncertainties; divine guidance is needed, which Moses calls ḥukm and is discussed at 26:83.
rows.anchor: prophets of God are of upright nature even before they are chosen by God as His envoys. However, mere upright nature and intellect are not enough

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers Pharaoh's claimed favor from 26:18–19: raising him does not entitle Pharaoh to enslave the Israelites or silence Moses' protest.
rows.anchor: this no doubt is a favour but it does not mean that Pharaoh has the right to enslave all the Israelites
